question: to the Commission Kathleen Van Brempt (S&D) Subject:

A new investigation by Global Echo entitled ‘Importing Occupation’12 analysed almost 6 000 Israeli agricultural shipments to Europe over eight years. It found that nearly one in five shipments to the EU originated in Israeli settlements. More than 16 % of the invoices that were examined declared the settlement goods to be of Israeli origin in order to obtain preferential tariff treatment under the EU-Israel Association Agreement, which included goods worth EUR 13.1 million that were ineligible for such treatment. The report found that even where preferential treatment is correctly denied by EU customs, the Israeli Government reimburses exporters, with at least EUR 63 million disbursed between 2005 and 2024. This compensation scheme renders the EU differentiation ineffective, even under full enforcement. 1.
What information does the Commission have about Israel’s compensation scheme for settlement exporters and has it assessed its impact on the EU differentiation policy?
Can the Commission confirm whether Israeli customs authorities continue to claim preferential treatment for settlement products and to declare them as being of Israeli origin?

Given that differentiation is neutralised by the exporter compensation scheme, how will the Commission ensure an effective trade policy that is consistent with international law? To that end, will the Commission propose a trade measure to prohibit the import of settlement products into the EU?
https://www.globalecho.law/importingoccupation/. https://www.globalecho.law/wp-content/uploads/2026/06/Global-Echo_Importing-Occupation_June2026_ENG.pdf. 1 2
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (1.9.2026) The Commission took note of the allegations made in the Global Echo report1 on the existence of a compensation scheme for exporters from illegal settlements in the Occupied Palestinian Territory (OPT) and the Golan Heights. Official information about the scheme is not publicly available since 2009. Israeli illegal settlements in the OPT are not part of Israel’s territory. Hence, trade with these settlements falls outside of the territorial scope of the EU – Israel Association Agreement2. Therefore, goods from the illegal settlements do not benefit from preferential treatment. The EU thereby differentiates between goods from Israel and from the illegal settlements upon importation and customs clearance, regardless of any potential ex post compensation. As explained in the reply to written question E-000112/20263, in accordance with a ‘Technical Arrangement’4 concluded by the EU and Israel, Member States' customs authorities are responsible for checking whether the postal codes appearing on Israeli proofs of origin, presented to them, correspond to any of the postal codes appearing in the list of noneligible locations made available to them by the Commission and refuse preference, where such is the case. Claims for preferential treatment are submitted by importers in a customs declaration. The customs administrations of the Member States verify the correctness of the data introduced in the import customs declaration. On 13 July 2026, at the Foreign Affairs Council, Member States discussed options for further trade-related measures vis-à-vis products originating in the settlements, as presented by the Commission, in accordance with the conclusions of the European Council of June 20265.
